steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from the 'react' module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode:
// Import React and useState from 'react' here

// Your component will go below
steps.expectedOutcome: The 'react' package is imported, making React and useState available for use in your component.
successCriteria: The code includes a valid import statement that imports both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the import statement needs adjustment. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import both React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Import createPortal from 'react-dom'
steps.instruction: Import the createPortal function from the 'react-dom' package.
steps.hint: Use a named import to bring createPortal into your component file.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing createPortal
import { createPortal } from 'react-dom';
steps.expectedOutcome: The createPortal function is imported and available for use in your component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported createPortal from react-dom. This function will allow you to render React children into a DOM node outside the parent component's hierarchy.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there's an issue with the import. Make sure you're importing createPortal from 'react-dom' using the correct syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import createPortal from the 'react-dom' package.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns JSX. Use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.hint:
Define a component that returns a JSX element. For example: `function App() { return
Hello
; }` or `const App = () => { return
Hello
; }`.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a functional component named App that returns JSX.
successCriteria: The code should define a component named App (either as a function or arrow function) that returns a JSX element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the App component. This is the foundation for building your portal example.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've defined a component named App that returns JSX. Check that you used the correct name and included a return statement with JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component is not properly defined. Ensure you create a functional component named App that returns JSX.

steps.title: Initialize modal open state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use the useState hook to create a state variable called isModalOpen, initialized to false. Make sure to properly type the state as boolean.
steps.hint: Remember to call useState<boolean>(false) and destructure the returned array into isModalOpen and setIsModalOpen.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have a typed boolean state variable isModalOpen initialized to false, ready to control modal visibility.
successCriteria: State is typed as boolean (either explicitly with <boolean> or inferred)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the modal state with proper TypeScript typing. The isModalOpen variable will track whether the portal should be visible.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Check that you've: 1) Used useState, 2) Named the variable isModalOpen, 3) Set initial value to false, and 4) Typed it as boolean (use useState<boolean>(false)).
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Inside the App component, you need to declare a state variable using useState. The state should be a boolean called isModalOpen starting as false.

steps.title: Define toggle modal handler
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, define a function named handleToggleModal that toggles the isModalOpen state.
steps.hint: Use the setModalOpen function from useState to update the state to the opposite of its current value.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleToggleModal function is defined that toggles the isModalOpen state between true and false.
successCriteria: The function should be defined inside the App component, use the setModalOpen state setter, and toggle the boolean value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the toggle handler. This function will be used to open and close the modal.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the function properly toggles the boolean state. Use the setModalOpen function to update the state to the opposite of its current value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The toggle handler isn't defined correctly. Remember to create a function that calls setModalOpen with the opposite of the current isModalOpen value.

steps.title: Create Modal component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named Modal that accepts children as props and returns a JSX element. Define it below the App component.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function. The component should have a parameter for props that includes children.
steps.expectedOutcome: A Modal component is defined that can accept children and will be used later for portal rendering.
successCriteria: The Modal component is defined with a function name 'Modal', accepts a children prop (typed as React.ReactNode), and returns a JSX element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the Modal component that accepts children. This component will serve as the content we'll render through a portal.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you name the component 'Modal'? Does it accept a children prop? Does it return JSX?
steps.feedbackWrong: The Modal component wasn't created correctly. Make sure to define a functional component named Modal that accepts children as a prop and returns JSX.

steps.title: Add portal target element in Modal
steps.instruction: Inside the Modal component, use createPortal to render its children to document.body. The Modal component should accept children as props and portal them outside the normal DOM hierarchy.
steps.hint: Call createPortal with two arguments: the children to render and the DOM element to mount them to (document.body).
steps.expectedOutcome: The Modal component now uses createPortal to render its content directly to document.body, enabling portal functionality.
successCriteria: createPortal is called with children as first argument
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented createPortal in the Modal component. This will render the modal content outside the normal React component hierarchy.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you're using createPortal correctly. Make sure to pass the children to render as the first argument and document.body as the second argument, and return the result.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Modal component doesn't seem to use createPortal correctly. Remember to call createPortal with the children and document.body, and return the result.

steps.title: Add main container structure
steps.instruction: In the App component's return statement, replace the existing div with a div that has className 'app-container'.
steps.hint: Update the JSX structure by changing the outer div's className attribute to 'app-container'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component returns a div element with className 'app-container' as its main container.
successCriteria: The outermost element is a div
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main container structure for the App component with the correct className.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the outermost element in the App component's return is a div with className 'app-container'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component should return a div with className 'app-container' as its main container. Check your return statement.

steps.title: Add toggle button
steps.instruction: Inside the App component's return statement, add a button element with the text 'Toggle Modal' and wire its onClick event to the toggle modal handler (which you'll need to define first if not already present).
steps.hint: Remember to define the handler function that toggles the isModalOpen state before using it in the button's onClick.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have a button that toggles the modal open/closed state when clicked.
successCriteria: onClick event handler defined and wired
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a toggle button that controls the modal visibility.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you have a button with the correct text and an onClick handler that toggles the isModalOpen state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The toggle button isn't quite right. Check that you have a button element with the text 'Toggle Modal' and an onClick handler that toggles the modal state.

steps.title: Conditionally render Modal
steps.instruction: In the App component's return statement, conditionally render the Modal component only when isModalOpen is true. You can use a ternary operator or logical AND (&&).
steps.hint: Use the isModalOpen state variable to control rendering. For example: {isModalOpen && <Modal />} or {isModalOpen ? <Modal /> : null}.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Modal component will only appear in the UI when isModalOpen is true, controlled by the state variable.
successCriteria: Conditional rendering logic in App's return
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added conditional rendering for the Modal component. The modal will now only appear when the state is true.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your conditional rendering syntax. Make sure you're using the isModalOpen state variable to control when the Modal component renders.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional rendering for the Modal component isn't quite right. Remember to use the isModalOpen state variable to control when the Modal component should appear in the UI.

steps.title: Add content to Modal
steps.instruction: Inside the Modal component, return a div element with modal content (e.g., a heading and a paragraph) as the children to be rendered via portal.
steps.hint: The Modal component should return JSX that will be passed to createPortal. Add a div with some content like a heading and text.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Modal component now returns a div with modal content, ready to be rendered via portal.
successCriteria: div contains at least one heading or paragraph element
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added content to the Modal component. This content will be rendered via portal in the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the Modal component returns a div with some content like a heading or paragraph.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Modal component should return JSX with a div containing modal content. Check that you're returning a valid JSX element.

steps.title: Add CSS for visual distinction
steps.instruction: Add a className 'modal-content' to the div inside your Modal component and style it with inline CSS to make it visually distinct from the main app content.
steps.hint: Add a className attribute to the div in the Modal component and use the style prop to give it a different background color, padding, and border.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Modal component's content div will have a className 'modal-content' and inline styles that make it visually distinct from the rest of the application.
successCriteria: The Modal component's return statement includes a div with className='modal-content'
The div has a style prop with at least backgroundColor, padding, and border properties
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added styling to make the modal content visually distinct. The className and inline styles will help users recognize portal content.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added both the className 'modal-content' and inline styles with at least backgroundColor, padding, and border properties to the div inside the Modal component.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on adding visual distinction to the modal content. Add a className 'modal-content' and inline styles to the div inside the Modal component to make it stand out from the main app content.
